instagram:
"Manufacturing operating system" sounds like a product category. It isn't.

No standards body defines it. Vendors use the same three words for four different things:

01 A way of managing: meetings, standard work, measures
02 A layer that connects the ERP and MES you already run
03 A newer kind of MES, close to the machines
04 One system that runs a small shop: stock, jobs, costs, quality

MRP, ERP and MES all have settled meanings. MOS has none, so the label tells you nothing about the product.

Full guide: link in bio.

Which meaning have you been pitched? Tell us below.

linkedin_profile:
ERP, MES, or "manufacturing operating system"?

I spent this week on that third phrase, and my honest conclusion is that on its own it can mean almost anything.

No standards body defines it. MRP, ERP and MES have settled meanings, and the ISA-95 standard places MES at level 3 and ERP at level 4. MOS appears nowhere.

When I read the pages that rank for the phrase, I found four different uses:

1. A way of managing the plant. Daily meetings, standard work, measures. Not software at all.
2. A layer that connects the ERP, MES and quality tools a plant already runs. Useful only when there are systems to connect.
3. A newer kind of MES, close to the machines and the operator.
4. One system that runs a small shop: stock, bills of materials, work orders, job costs, purchasing and quality in one place.

We build ZMOS, so we use the phrase ourselves, in the fourth sense. For a shop of 10 to 50 people still on spreadsheets and paper travellers, that is usually what's needed. A plant with an established ERP and connected machines is a different buyer.

My advice: ignore the category name. Ask which records the system holds, where its shop-floor data comes from, and what it replaces. Then ask the vendor to show one job from quote to invoice.

I've put the full comparison and eight questions for vendors in the guide (link in the first comment).

What has a software label promised you that the product didn't deliver?

linkedin_page:
Four products can carry the label "manufacturing operating system" and do four different jobs.

That is the finding of our new guide. The phrase has no standard definition, unlike MRP, ERP and MES, which sit in long-settled meanings and, for ERP and MES, in the ISA-95 model.

What vendors and consultants mean by it:
• A management system of routines and measures
• A software layer over existing ERP and MES
• A newer style of MES with planning and machine data
• A single system for a small shop's stock, jobs, costs and quality

The guide maps each meaning to the type of business it suits, places them on the ISA-95 levels, and lists eight questions to put to any vendor. The most important: can you show one job, from quote to invoice, in your product today?

Full guide in the first comment.
